clinicalPearls: Weakness of the superior oblique produces vertical and torsional diplopia that is worse on looking down and in, as when reading or descending stairs
Patients typically adopt a compensatory head tilt away from the affected side to control the diplopia
The Parks-Bielschowsky three-step test localises the palsy and shows worsening hypertropia on head tilt toward the affected side
It is the commonest cause of vertical diplopia and, because the nerve is thin with a long course, is frequently caused by head trauma
Congenital fourth nerve palsy is common and may decompensate in adulthood; old photographs showing a long-standing head tilt support this
Bilateral palsies, often traumatic, cause alternating hypertropia and prominent torsion
reference.pathophysiology: The trochlear nerve supplies the superior oblique, which intorts, depresses and abducts the eye; its palsy leaves the eye relatively elevated and extorted with impaired depression in adduction. The nerve is uniquely long, thin and the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally after decussating, crossing the tentorial edge, which makes it especially susceptible to closed head injury. Microvascular ischaemia is another common cause, while congenital laxity or absence of the tendon can present later when fusional reserves that had compensated finally fail.
additionalDifferentials: Thyroid eye disease affecting the inferior rectus
Orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus restriction
additionalInvestigations: Orthoptic assessment with the three-step test and measurement of torsion
Comparison with old photographs for a long-standing head tilt
MRI of the brain and orbits when the palsy is not clearly traumatic or vasculopathic
Acetylcholine-receptor antibody testing if myasthenia is possible
redFlags: Additional neurological signs or other cranial neuropathies
Bilateral palsy without a clear traumatic explanation
Features suggesting skew deviation from posterior fossa disease
reference.prognosis: Microvascular and many traumatic palsies improve over weeks to months; decompensated congenital and persistent palsies are well managed with prisms or superior oblique strengthening or other strabismus surgery.
pitfalls: Confusing a decompensated congenital palsy with a new acquired lesion
Overlooking skew deviation as a mimic of vertical diplopia
Missing subtle torsion that helps localise the palsy
Attributing bilateral palsy to a unilateral cause
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Treat the underlying cause, optimising vascular risk factors in microvascular palsy and managing any lesion identified on imaging
Observe microvascular and many traumatic palsies, which commonly recover over weeks to months
Relieve diplopia symptomatically with Fresnel or ground-in prisms, or temporary monocular occlusion
Refer for strabismus surgery such as superior oblique strengthening or inferior oblique weakening when the deviation is stable but persistent
Recognise and treat decompensated congenital palsy, supported by old photographs, with prisms or surgery
Coordinate orthoptic, ophthalmology and neurology follow-up to monitor recovery and re-image if the palsy progresses or fails to resolve
